And the mountains were mountains of bronze.<sup>2</sup>The first chariot had red horses, the second black horses,<sup>3</sup>the third white horses, and the fourth chariot dappled horses—all of them strong.<sup>4</sup>Then I answered and said to the angel who talked with me, "What are these, my lord?"<sup>5</sup>And the angel answered and said to me, "These are going out to the four winds of heaven, after presenting themselves before the Lord of all the earth.<sup>6</sup>The chariot with the black horses goes toward the north country, the white ones go after them, and the dappled ones go toward the south country."<sup>7</sup>When the strong horses came out, they were impatient to go and patrol the earth. And he said, "Go, patrol the earth." So they patrolled the earth.<sup>8</sup>Then he cried to me, "Behold, those who go toward the north country have set my Spirit at rest in the north country."<sup>9</sup>And the word of the LORD came to me:<sup>10</sup>"Take from the exiles Heldai, Tobijah, and Jedaiah, who have arrived from Babylon, and go the same day to the house of Josiah, the son of Zephaniah.<sup>11</sup>Take from them silver and gold, and make a crown, and set it on the head of Joshua, the son of Jehozadak, the high priest.<sup>12</sup>And say to him, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, "Behold, the man whose name is the Branch: for he shall branch out from his place, and he shall build the temple of the LORD.<sup>13</sup>It is he who shall build the temple of the LORD and shall bear royal honor, and shall sit and rule on his throne. And there shall be a priest on his throne, and the counsel of peace shall be between them both."'<sup>14</sup>And the crown shall be in the temple of the LORD as a reminder to Helem, Tobijah, Jedaiah, and Hen the son of Zephaniah.<sup>15</sup>"And those who are far off shall come and help to build the temple of the LORD. And you shall know that the LORD of hosts has sent me to you. And this shall come to pass, if you will diligently obey the voice of the LORD your God."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Four chariots come out from between two mountains ... of bronze, with red, black, white and dappled horses (vv. 1-3). They are going out to the four winds of heaven, after presenting themselves before the Lord of all the earth (vv. 4-5). They patrol the earth, and word comes back that those who went north have set my Spirit at rest in the north country (vv. 6-8).
verseByVerse.theology: God's patrols go out from his presence to every direction, and his purposes are at rest only when justice is done.

verseByVerse.quote: Again I lifted my eyes and saw, and behold, four chariots came out from between two mountains. And the mountains were mountains of bronze. The first chariot had red horses, the second black horses, the third white horses, and the fourth chariot dappled horses—all of them strong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Again I lifted my eyes and saw, and behold, four chariots came out from between two mountains. And the mountains were mountains of bronze.

The last of the eight night visions, and it answers the first. Chapter 1 opened with horsemen reporting that the world was quiet while God's people suffered. Now chariots come out, and chariots are for war.

They come from between two mountains ... of bronze. Bronze gates and bronze mountains suggest a fixed, immovable place: the throne room from which God's decisions issue.

The first chariot had red horses, the second black horses,

the third white horses, and the fourth chariot dappled horses—all of them strong.

Four chariots with differently coloured teams (the ESV notes the last line may read "the fourth chariot strong dappled horses"). Revelation's four horsemen draw on this imagery. Zechariah is not told what the colours mean, and neither are we.

Four is the Bible's number for the whole world: four winds, four corners. Whatever these teams are, they cover everything, and they are all under one command.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I answered and said to the angel who talked with me, "What are these, my lord?" And the angel answered and said to me, "These are going out to the four winds of heaven, after presenting themselves before the Lord of all the earth. The chariot with the black horses goes toward the north country, the white ones go after them, and the dappled ones go toward the south country." When the strong horses came out, they were impatient to go and patrol the earth. And he said, "Go, patrol the earth." So they patrolled the earth. Then he cried to me, "Behold, those who go toward the north country have set my Spirit at rest in the north country."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I answered and said to the angel who talked with me, "What are these, my lord?"

And the angel answered and said to me, "These are going out to the four winds of heaven, after presenting themselves before the Lord of all the earth.

Here is the explanation that matters. They go to the four winds of heaven, that is, in every direction, and they go after presenting themselves before the Lord of all the earth (the ESV notes an alternative, "These are the four winds of heaven going out").

Nothing in this vision moves until it has stood before God. The forces at work in world history, whatever they are, report for orders first. That is precisely what a small, vulnerable community needed to know.

The chariot with the black horses goes toward the north country, the white ones go after them, and the dappled ones go toward the south country."

When the strong horses came out, they were impatient to go and patrol the earth. And he said, "Go, patrol the earth." So they patrolled the earth.

The horses are impatient to go. God's agents are not reluctant; they strain at the bit while he holds them until the hour comes. We often mistake God's timing for God's inactivity.

Then he cried to me, "Behold, those who go toward the north country have set my Spirit at rest in the north country."

The north country is Babylon, the direction from which invaders always came and where the exiles had been taken. When God's judgment has been carried out there, his Spirit is at rest.

That is a striking way to speak. God is not restless with anxiety, but he is not indifferent either; his purposes press on until wrongs are dealt with, and then there is rest. The same will be true on the last day.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–15 — A Crown for the Priest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zechariah is told to take silver and gold from men newly arrived from Babylon, and make a crown, and set it on the head of Joshua ... the high priest (vv. 9-11). The word that goes with it looks far beyond Joshua: Behold, the man whose name is the Branch, who shall build the temple of the LORD, shall bear royal honor, and there shall be a priest on his throne (vv. 12-13). The crown is kept in the temple as a reminder, and those who are far off shall come and help to build (vv. 14-15).
verseByVerse.theology: God crowns a priest as a sign of the coming one who will be king and priest together, and who builds his temple with people from far away.

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of the LORD came to me: "Take from the exiles Heldai, Tobijah, and Jedaiah, who have arrived from Babylon, and go the same day to the house of Josiah, the son of Zephaniah. Take from them silver and gold, and make a crown, and set it on the head of Joshua, the son of Jehozadak, the high priest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the word of the LORD came to me:

"Take from the exiles Heldai, Tobijah, and Jedaiah, who have arrived from Babylon, and go the same day to the house of Josiah, the son of Zephaniah.

The visions end and an action begins. Three men have arrived from Babylon, presumably carrying gifts from Jews still there. Zechariah is to go the same day; this is urgent.

Take from them silver and gold, and make a crown, and set it on the head of Joshua, the son of Jehozadak, the high priest.

Now the surprise, and it is easy to miss how shocking it is. A crown is made, and it is placed on the head of the high priest.

In Israel those two offices were kept strictly apart. Kings came from Judah and David; priests came from Levi and Aaron. When King Uzziah tried to burn incense in the temple he was struck with leprosy (2 Chr 26:16-21). Here, by God's own instruction, a crown goes on a priest's head.

Zerubbabel, the descendant of David, is standing right there and is not crowned. This is a deliberate sign, and Zechariah is told what it signifies.

And notice where the crown came from: the gifts of exiles who had not come home. Believers far away, who would never see this temple, paid for the sign that pointed to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: And say to him, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, "Behold, the man whose name is the Branch: for he shall branch out from his place, and he shall build the temple of the LORD. It is he who shall build the temple of the LORD and shall bear royal honor, and shall sit and rule on his throne. And there shall be a priest on his throne, and the counsel of peace shall be between them both."'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And say to him, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, "Behold, the man whose name is the Branch: for he shall branch out from his place, and he shall build the temple of the LORD.

The Branch again (3:8), the promised king from David's cut-down family tree. Joshua is wearing the crown; the Branch is the one it points to. He shall build the temple of the LORD — not this modest building, which Zerubbabel's hands would finish, but a greater one.

It is he who shall build the temple of the LORD and shall bear royal honor, and shall sit and rule on his throne. And there shall be a priest on his throne, and the counsel of peace shall be between them both."'

Read that slowly. One man will bear royal honor and sit and rule on his throne, and at the same time be a priest on his throne. The two offices that Israel had kept apart for a thousand years are joined in one person. (The ESV notes the last phrase may be read "between him and the LORD".)

The Psalms had hinted at this: a king in David's line addressed as a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek (Ps 110:4), remembering the ancient figure who was both king of Salem and priest of God Most High. Hebrews takes it up and applies it all to Jesus, who holds his priesthood permanently and is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him (Heb 7:24-25).

This is the heart of the chapter and one of the clearest pictures of Christ in the prophets. We need a king to rule us and a priest to reconcile us, and it would be a poor arrangement if they were two different people who had to agree. In Jesus the counsel of peace is settled in one person: the one who brings us to God is the one who governs us.

verseByVerse.quote: And the crown shall be in the temple of the LORD as a reminder to Helem, Tobijah, Jedaiah, and Hen the son of Zephaniah. "And those who are far off shall come and help to build the temple of the LORD. And you shall know that the LORD of hosts has sent me to you. And this shall come to pass, if you will diligently obey the voice of the LORD your God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the crown shall be in the temple of the LORD as a reminder to Helem, Tobijah, Jedaiah, and Hen the son of Zephaniah.

The crown does not stay on Joshua's head. It is placed in the temple as a reminder, hanging there as a promise waiting to be kept. (The ESV notes that Helem is another spelling of Heldai in verse 10.)

The men who gave the silver and gold are named twice in this passage, which is a kindness. Their contribution was money and a long journey, and God put their names in his book.

"And those who are far off shall come and help to build the temple of the LORD. And you shall know that the LORD of hosts has sent me to you. And this shall come to pass, if you will diligently obey the voice of the LORD your God."

The men from Babylon are a sample of something larger: those who are far off shall come and help to build. The builders of God's true temple will include people from a long way away.

Paul uses that very language of Gentile Christians: you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ, and are now built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit (Eph 2:13, 22). Every believer with no Jewish blood is one of the far-off people helping to build the temple Zechariah saw.

The chapter closes with a condition: if you will diligently obey. God's promises are certain, and the enjoyment of them is bound up with obedience. The crown is in the temple; the question for each generation is whether they will live as people who believe the one it points to is coming.

6.title: The Crown and the Branch
6.overview:
Four chariots come out from between two mountains of bronze, with red, black, white and dappled horses (vv. 1-3). They are the four winds of heaven going out after presenting themselves before the Lord of all the earth; the black horses go north, the white after them and the dappled south (vv. 4-6). The strong horses are impatient to patrol the earth, and word comes that those going north have set God's Spirit at rest in the north country (vv. 7-8).

Then the word of the LORD tells Zechariah to take silver and gold from exiles newly arrived from Babylon, make a crown, and set it on the head of Joshua the high priest (vv. 9-11). He is to say: behold, the man whose name is the Branch, who will branch out from his place and build the temple of the LORD; he will bear royal honour and sit and rule on his throne, and there will be a priest on his throne, with the counsel of peace between them both (vv. 12-13).

The crown is to be kept in the temple as a reminder to the donors (v. 14), and those who are far off will come and help to build the temple of the LORD, which will come to pass if they diligently obey the voice of the LORD their God (v. 15).
6.theology:
The powers at work in world history move only after reporting before the Lord of all the earth (v. 5).

God's agents are eager and his timing is deliberate; his apparent delay is not inactivity (v. 7).

God's purposes press on until wrong is dealt with, and then there is rest (v. 8).

A crown on a priest's head breaks Israel's settled order, as a deliberate sign of something new (v. 11; 2 Chr 26:16-21).

The Branch will be king and priest in one person, so that the one who reconciles us is the one who rules us (v. 13; Ps 110:4; Heb 7:24-25).

God records the names of those whose gifts support his work (v. 14).

People from far away help to build God's true temple, fulfilled in the Gentiles brought near in Christ (v. 15; Eph 2:13, 22).
6.examples:
Chariots issuing from between two mountains of bronze.

Horses straining at the bit until God says go.

A crown of silver and gold made from an offering carried out of Babylon.

A crown placed on the head of a priest, with the king standing by.

Two offices kept apart for a thousand years, joined in one man.

A crown hung in the temple as a reminder of a promise.

Far-off people arriving to help build.

7.text: <sup>1</sup>In the fourth year of King Darius, the word of the LORD came to Zechariah on the fourth day of the ninth month, which is Chislev.<sup>2</sup>Now the people of Bethel had sent Sharezer and Regem-melech and their men to entreat the favor of the LORD,<sup>3</sup>saying to the priests of the house of the LORD of hosts and the prophets, "Should I weep and abstain in the fifth month, as I have done for so many years?"<sup>4</sup>Then the word of the LORD of hosts came to me:<sup>5</sup>"Say to all the people of the land and the priests, 'When you fasted and mourned in the fifth month and in the seventh, for these seventy years, was it for me that you fasted?<sup>6</sup>And when you eat and when you drink, do you not eat for yourselves and drink for yourselves?<sup>7</sup>Were not these the words that the LORD proclaimed by the former prophets, when Jerusalem was inhabited and prosperous, with her cities around her, and the South and the lowland were inhabited?'"<sup>8</sup>And the word of the LORD came to Zechariah, saying,<sup>9</sup>"Thus says the LORD of hosts, Render true judgments, show kindness and mercy to one another,<sup>10</sup>do not oppress the widow, the fatherless, the sojourner, or the poor, and let none of you devise evil against another in your heart."<sup>11</sup>But they refused to pay attention and turned a stubborn shoulder and stopped their ears that they might not hear.<sup>12</sup>They made their hearts diamond-hard lest they should hear the law and the words that the LORD of hosts had sent by his Spirit through the former prophets. Therefore great anger came from the LORD of hosts.<sup>13</sup>"As I called, and they would not hear, so they called, and I would not hear," says the LORD of hosts,<sup>14</sup>"and I scattered them with a whirlwind among all the nations that they had not known. Thus the land they left was desolate, so that no one went to and fro, and the pleasant land was made desolate."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two years after the visions, men come from Bethel to ask the priests whether they should keep fasting in the fifth month as they have for so many years (vv. 1-3). God answers with a question of his own: When you fasted and mourned ... was it for me that you fasted? and, when you eat and drink, is that not for yourselves? (vv. 4-6). The former prophets had said all this when the city was still prosperous (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: God asks of every religious habit the one question that matters: who is it for?

verseByVerse.quote: In the fourth year of King Darius, the word of the LORD came to Zechariah on the fourth day of the ninth month, which is Chislev. Now the people of Bethel had sent Sharezer and Regem-melech and their men to entreat the favor of the LORD, saying to the priests of the house of the LORD of hosts and the prophets, "Should I weep and abstain in the fifth month, as I have done for so many years?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the fourth year of King Darius, the word of the LORD came to Zechariah on the fourth day of the ninth month, which is Chislev.

Two years have passed since the night visions. It is now 518 BC, the temple is rising, and the mood has changed from despair to something like normality.

Now the people of Bethel had sent Sharezer and Regem-melech and their men to entreat the favor of the LORD,

saying to the priests of the house of the LORD of hosts and the prophets, "Should I weep and abstain in the fifth month, as I have done for so many years?"

A delegation arrives with a practical question. During the exile the people had kept several fasts mourning the disasters. The fast of the fifth month marked the burning of the temple by the Babylonians (2 Kgs 25:8-9). Now the temple is nearly rebuilt. Should the mourning continue?

It is a reasonable question, the kind any church committee might ask: we have always done this; do we still need to? And notice they ask about a fast God never commanded. It was their own tradition, seventy years old and deeply felt.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD of hosts came to me: "Say to all the people of the land and the priests, 'When you fasted and mourned in the fifth month and in the seventh, for these seventy years, was it for me that you fasted? And when you eat and when you drink, do you not eat for yourselves and drink for yourselves? Were not these the words that the LORD proclaimed by the former prophets, when Jerusalem was inhabited and prosperous, with her cities around her, and the South and the lowland were inhabited?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the word of the LORD of hosts came to me:

"Say to all the people of the land and the priests, 'When you fasted and mourned in the fifth month and in the seventh, for these seventy years, was it for me that you fasted?

God does not answer the question they asked. He asks a better one: was it for me that you fasted?

Seventy years of genuine grief, and God queries the direction of it. They had mourned a burnt building and a lost country and their own suffering. Had they mourned their sin? Had the fasting been aimed at God at all, or had it been a national ritual of self-pity?

That question can be asked of any religious habit. The quiet time, the church attendance, the giving, the abstaining: who is it for? It is perfectly possible to do genuinely costly religious things for reasons that have nothing to do with God.

And when you eat and when you drink, do you not eat for yourselves and drink for yourselves?

The same test applied to ordinary life. If our fasting is for ourselves and our feasting is for ourselves, then everything is for ourselves, and God has not really come into it. Paul puts the positive version: whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God (1 Cor 10:31).

Were not these the words that the LORD proclaimed by the former prophets, when Jerusalem was inhabited and prosperous, with her cities around her, and the South and the lowland were inhabited?'"

God points them back to the prophets who preached before the exile, when everything was still standing. The message has not changed, and the tragedy is that they are asking about fast days rather than about the thing the prophets actually pressed, which the next verses spell out.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — The Words They Would Not Hear
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The word God had sent by the former prophets was plain: Render true judgments, show kindness and mercy to one another, and do not oppress the widow, the fatherless, the sojourner, or the poor (vv. 8-10). But they turned a stubborn shoulder, stopped their ears and made their hearts diamond-hard (vv. 11-12). So God says, As I called, and they would not hear, so they called, and I would not hear, and the pleasant land was left desolate (vv. 13-14).
verseByVerse.theology: God wanted mercy and justice, not mourning ceremonies, and refusing to listen finally silences the answer.

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of the LORD came to Zechariah, saying, "Thus says the LORD of hosts, Render true judgments, show kindness and mercy to one another, do not oppress the widow, the fatherless, the sojourner, or the poor, and let none of you devise evil against another in your heart."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the word of the LORD came to Zechariah, saying,

"Thus says the LORD of hosts, Render true judgments, show kindness and mercy to one another,

do not oppress the widow, the fatherless, the sojourner, or the poor, and let none of you devise evil against another in your heart."

Here is what God had always wanted, and it is startlingly concrete.

Render true judgments: honest decisions in court and in daily dealings. Show kindness and mercy to one another: the warm, practical goodness that makes a community liveable. Then the four groups: the widow, the fatherless, the sojourner and the poor — the people with no husband, no father, no citizenship and no money, the four classic ways of being defenceless in that world.

And finally the inward command: let none of you devise evil against another in your heart. God legislates for the imagination, because that is where injustice is designed.

Micah had summarised it: to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God (Mic 6:8). James says religion that is pure is to visit orphans and widows in their affliction (Jas 1:27). The test of real religion has never changed, and it is never merely a matter of what we abstain from.

verseByVerse.quote: But they refused to pay attention and turned a stubborn shoulder and stopped their ears that they might not hear. They made their hearts diamond-hard lest they should hear the law and the words that the LORD of hosts had sent by his Spirit through the former prophets. Therefore great anger came from the LORD of hosts. "As I called, and they would not hear, so they called, and I would not hear," says the LORD of hosts, "and I scattered them with a whirlwind among all the nations that they had not known. Thus the land they left was desolate, so that no one went to and fro, and the pleasant land was made desolate."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they refused to pay attention and turned a stubborn shoulder and stopped their ears that they might not hear.

Three pictures of refusal, and they get steadily worse. They refused to pay attention. They turned a stubborn shoulder, the image of an ox wrenching its shoulder out from under the yoke. And they stopped their ears (the ESV notes the Hebrew is "made their ears too heavy to hear").

They made their hearts diamond-hard lest they should hear the law and the words that the LORD of hosts had sent by his Spirit through the former prophets. Therefore great anger came from the LORD of hosts.

Now the deepest level: they made their hearts diamond-hard. Note the verb. Nobody did it to them. Hardness of heart is manufactured, decision by decision, until nothing gets in.

And notice what they were refusing: words that the LORD of hosts had sent by his Spirit. Rejecting the prophets was not merely ignoring good advice.

There is only one cure for a diamond-hard heart, and it is not effort. God promises it elsewhere: I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh (Ezek 36:26). What we cannot soften, he can replace.

"As I called, and they would not hear, so they called, and I would not hear," says the LORD of hosts,

A terrible symmetry. (The ESV notes the Hebrew has "he" where the ESV supplies says the LORD of hosts.) The generation that would not listen eventually needed God to listen, and found silence.

This is not God sulking. It is the settled consequence of a life lived deaf to him. It is also why every call of God should be treated as urgent while it can still be heard.

"and I scattered them with a whirlwind among all the nations that they had not known. Thus the land they left was desolate, so that no one went to and fro, and the pleasant land was made desolate."

The chapter ends bleakly: a whirlwind, exile among strangers, and a pleasant land left empty.

And that is the answer to the delegation's question about fasting. You are asking whether to keep mourning the ruin. Ask instead why the ruin happened, and make sure that this generation is not like the last. Then read chapter 8, where God turns all four fasts into feasts.

7.title: Was It for Me That You Fasted?
7.overview:
In the fourth year of Darius, men from Bethel come to ask the priests and prophets whether they should go on weeping and abstaining in the fifth month as they have for so many years (vv. 1-3). God replies with a question: when they fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh months for seventy years, was it for him that they fasted? And when they eat and drink, do they not do it for themselves? The former prophets had said these things when Jerusalem was still inhabited and prosperous (vv. 4-7).

The word of the LORD had been plain: render true judgments, show kindness and mercy to one another, do not oppress the widow, the fatherless, the sojourner or the poor, and do not devise evil against one another in the heart (vv. 8-10). But they refused to pay attention, turned a stubborn shoulder, stopped their ears and made their hearts diamond-hard so that they would not hear the law and the words God sent by his Spirit through the prophets; so great anger came from the LORD (vv. 11-12). As he called and they would not hear, so they called and he would not hear; he scattered them with a whirlwind among nations they did not know, and the pleasant land was left desolate (vv. 13-14).
7.theology:
God questions the direction of our religious habits: who are they actually for? (vv. 5-6).

Costly religious activity can be entirely self-centred (vv. 5-6; 1 Cor 10:31).

What God has always wanted is true judgment, kindness and mercy, and protection for the defenceless (vv. 9-10; Mic 6:8; Jas 1:27).

God's commands reach the imagination, where injustice is designed (v. 10).

Hardness of heart is manufactured by repeated refusals, and only God can replace such a heart (vv. 11-12; Ezek 36:26).

Persistent refusal to hear God ends in the silence of unanswered prayer (v. 13).
7.examples:
A delegation asking whether a seventy-year-old tradition can now stop.

A question answered with a better question.

Fasting for ourselves and feasting for ourselves, with God in neither.

Four kinds of defenceless people named in one sentence.

An ox wrenching its shoulder out from under the yoke.

Hearts made as hard as diamond, one refusal at a time.

A generation that would not hear, and then was not heard.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — I Have Returned to Zion
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I am jealous for Zion with great jealousy (vv. 1-2). I have returned to Zion and will dwell in the midst of Jerusalem, which will be called the faithful city (v. 3). The promise is beautifully ordinary: Old men and old women shall again sit in the streets and the streets of the city shall be full of boys and girls playing (vv. 4-5). If that seems marvelous to the remnant, should it seem marvellous to God? (v. 6). He will bring his people home, and they shall be my people, and I will be their God (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: God's promise of restoration is measured in old people sitting safely and children playing in the street.

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of the LORD of hosts came, saying, "Thus says the LORD of hosts: I am jealous for Zion with great jealousy, and I am jealous for her with great wrath. Thus says the LORD: I have returned to Zion and will dwell in the midst of Jerusalem, and Jerusalem shall be called the faithful city, and the mountain of the LORD of hosts, the holy mountain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the word of the LORD of hosts came, saying,

"Thus says the LORD of hosts: I am jealous for Zion with great jealousy, and I am jealous for her with great wrath.

Chapter 7 ended in desolation. Chapter 8 answers it with ten messages, each beginning Thus says the LORD of hosts, and the first is about God's feelings. He is jealous for Zion, the fierce protectiveness of a husband who will not share his wife or let her be harmed.

Thus says the LORD: I have returned to Zion and will dwell in the midst of Jerusalem, and Jerusalem shall be called the faithful city, and the mountain of the LORD of hosts, the holy mountain.

I have returned to Zion: the promise of 1:16 restated. And the city will get a new name, the faithful city. Isaiah had cried, How the faithful city has become a whore (Isa 1:21). God intends to give the title back.

Notice that God speaks of returning. The city had not been abandoned by him for ever, and the word "again" will keep coming back through this chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD of hosts: Old men and old women shall again sit in the streets of Jerusalem, each with staff in hand because of great age. And the streets of the city shall be full of boys and girls playing in its streets. Thus says the LORD of hosts: If it is marvelous in the sight of the remnant of this people in those days, should it also be marvelous in my sight, declares the LORD of hosts? Thus says the LORD of hosts: Behold, I will save my people from the east country and from the west country, and I will bring them to dwell in the midst of Jerusalem. And they shall be my people, and I will be their God, in faithfulness and in righteousness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the LORD of hosts: Old men and old women shall again sit in the streets of Jerusalem, each with staff in hand because of great age.

And the streets of the city shall be full of boys and girls playing in its streets.

Here is one of the loveliest pictures of peace in the Bible, and notice how ordinary it is. Not victory parades or gold: old men and old women sitting out in the street with their walking sticks, and boys and girls playing.

Both groups are the ones who suffer first when a society is violent. Old people stay indoors; children are kept inside. A city where the very old sit safely in public and children play in the street is a city at peace. That is what God promises, and it shows what God counts as a great blessing.

Thus says the LORD of hosts: If it is marvelous in the sight of the remnant of this people in those days, should it also be marvelous in my sight, declares the LORD of hosts?

To the little community it all seemed impossible. God's reply is gentle: it may look marvelous, that is, impossible, to you; must it therefore be impossible to me? The same question was asked of Abraham and Sarah, and the angel said to Mary, nothing will be impossible with God (Luke 1:37).

Thus says the LORD of hosts: Behold, I will save my people from the east country and from the west country,

and I will bring them to dwell in the midst of Jerusalem. And they shall be my people, and I will be their God, in faithfulness and in righteousness."

God will gather them from every direction, and the covenant words return: they shall be my people, and I will be their God. That sentence runs through the Bible, from Sinai to the new covenant (Jer 31:33) and on to the last page, where God dwells with his people forever (Rev 21:3).

And the two words at the end matter: in faithfulness and in righteousness. This is not sentimental restoration; God does it honestly, which for us means through the cross.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–17 — Let Your Hands Be Strong
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Let your hands be strong, says God to the builders (v. 9). Before, there was no wage and no safety (v. 10), but now there will be a sowing of peace and a fruitful land (vv. 11-12). As you have been a byword of cursing among the nations ... so will I save you, and you shall be a blessing. Fear not (v. 13). As God once purposed disaster, so now he has purposed good (vv. 14-15). And so: Speak the truth to one another, judge truly, devise no evil, love no false oath (vv. 16-17).
verseByVerse.theology: God's promised blessing comes with a plain ethic: truthful speech, honest courts and no scheming.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD of hosts: "Let your hands be strong, you who in these days have been hearing these words from the mouth of the prophets who were present on the day that the foundation of the house of the LORD of hosts was laid, that the temple might be built. For before those days there was no wage for man or any wage for beast, neither was there any safety from the foe for him who went out or came in, for I set every man against his neighbor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the LORD of hosts: "Let your hands be strong, you who in these days have been hearing these words from the mouth of the prophets who were present on the day that the foundation of the house of the LORD of hosts was laid, that the temple might be built.

Let your hands be strong: the encouragement of a foreman to tired builders. And the reason is that they are hearing God's promises while the work is in progress. Promises are given to be worked by.

For before those days there was no wage for man or any wage for beast, neither was there any safety from the foe for him who went out or came in, for I set every man against his neighbor.

This is Haggai's diagnosis (Hag 1:6-11) in a sentence: no wages, no security, no neighbourliness. And God takes responsibility for it: I set every man against his neighbor. When a community turns from God, the fractures between people are part of the judgment.

Hard years have a way of teaching people to expect nothing else. God addresses that directly in the next verse.

verseByVerse.quote: But now I will not deal with the remnant of this people as in the former days, declares the LORD of hosts. For there shall be a sowing of peace. The vine shall give its fruit, and the ground shall give its produce, and the heavens shall give their dew. And I will cause the remnant of this people to possess all these things. And as you have been a byword of cursing among the nations, O house of Judah and house of Israel, so will I save you, and you shall be a blessing. Fear not, but let your hands be strong."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But now I will not deal with the remnant of this people as in the former days, declares the LORD of hosts.

For there shall be a sowing of peace. The vine shall give its fruit, and the ground shall give its produce, and the heavens shall give their dew. And I will cause the remnant of this people to possess all these things.

But now. Two of the best words in Scripture. A sowing of peace: the seed goes in and what comes up is peace. Vine, ground and heavens all cooperate again.

And as you have been a byword of cursing among the nations, O house of Judah and house of Israel, so will I save you, and you shall be a blessing. Fear not, but let your hands be strong."

The reversal is complete. They had been a byword of cursing, the nation other nations pointed at as an example of ruin. Now: you shall be a blessing, which was God's word to Abraham at the very beginning.

And the practical conclusion comes twice in this chapter: Fear not, but let your hands be strong. God's promises are not an invitation to sit still.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD of hosts: "As I purposed to bring disaster to you when your fathers provoked me to wrath, and I did not relent, says the LORD of hosts, so again have I purposed in these days to bring good to Jerusalem and to the house of Judah; fear not. These are the things that you shall do: Speak the truth to one another; render in your gates judgments that are true and make for peace; do not devise evil in your hearts against one another, and love no false oath, for all these things I hate, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For thus says the LORD of hosts: "As I purposed to bring disaster to you when your fathers provoked me to wrath, and I did not relent, says the LORD of hosts,

so again have I purposed in these days to bring good to Jerusalem and to the house of Judah; fear not.

God argues from his own track record, and it is a surprising argument. You know I do what I say, because I did the terrible thing I promised and did not relent. The exile proved that God's word holds. Therefore, when he promises good, expect the same reliability.

A believer can use this. The sharpest evidence that God keeps his word may be some discipline we have been through. The God who was that serious about his warnings is that serious about his promises.

These are the things that you shall do: Speak the truth to one another; render in your gates judgments that are true and make for peace;

do not devise evil in your hearts against one another, and love no false oath, for all these things I hate, declares the LORD."

And here is the response God asks for, and it is startlingly down to earth. Speak the truth to one another. Paul quotes this line to the church at Ephesus as basic Christian behaviour. Judge truly in the courts, and in judgments that make for peace, because justice is meant to heal a community, not merely to settle scores.

Then the heart again: do not devise evil in your hearts, and no false oaths, for all these things I hate. Notice what God says he hates. Here they are lies, crooked judgments, private scheming and perjury — sins of ordinary people in ordinary dealings.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The fasts of the fourth, fifth, seventh and tenth months shall be to the house of Judah seasons of joy and gladness and cheerful feasts. Therefore love truth and peace (vv. 18-19). Peoples from many cities will urge one another, Let us go at once to entreat the favor of the LORD (vv. 20-22), and ten men from the nations of every tongue shall take hold of the robe of a Jew, saying, 'Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you' (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: God turns his people's mourning into feasting, and makes them the people others follow to find him.

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of the LORD of hosts came to me, saying, "Thus says the LORD of hosts: The fast of the fourth month and the fast of the fifth and the fast of the seventh and the fast of the tenth shall be to the house of Judah seasons of joy and gladness and cheerful feasts. Therefore love truth and peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the word of the LORD of hosts came to me, saying,

"Thus says the LORD of hosts: The fast of the fourth month and the fast of the fifth and the fast of the seventh and the fast of the tenth shall be to the house of Judah seasons of joy and gladness and cheerful feasts. Therefore love truth and peace.

Now, at last, the delegation from chapter 7 gets its answer. They asked whether they should keep one fast. God answers about all four, and he does not say "stop". He says they will become seasons of joy and gladness and cheerful feasts.

That is how God deals with his people's grief. He does not tell them to forget it or to keep observing it forever; he turns it into gladness. The days that marked the worst events in their history become festivals.

Christians know the greatest instance of this. The day of the most terrible event in history is called Good Friday.

And notice the condition attached: Therefore love truth and peace. Not "keep the right feasts", but love the things God loves.

And the God who can do that with a calendar can do it with a life. Anniversaries that have been dreaded for years are not beyond his reach.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the LORD of hosts: Peoples shall yet come, even the inhabitants of many cities. The inhabitants of one city shall go to another, saying, 'Let us go at once to entreat the favor of the LORD and to seek the LORD of hosts; I myself am going.' Many peoples and strong nations shall come to seek the LORD of hosts in Jerusalem and to entreat the favor of the LORD. Thus says the LORD of hosts: In those days ten men from the nations of every tongue shall take hold of the robe of a Jew, saying, 'Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Thus says the LORD of hosts: Peoples shall yet come, even the inhabitants of many cities.

The inhabitants of one city shall go to another, saying, 'Let us go at once to entreat the favor of the LORD and to seek the LORD of hosts; I myself am going.'

Watch the scene. People in one city call on their neighbours in the next: Let us go at once, and then the personal commitment, I myself am going. Nobody is coerced. This is the spread of genuine spiritual hunger, and it begins with individuals who will not wait.

Many peoples and strong nations shall come to seek the LORD of hosts in Jerusalem and to entreat the favor of the LORD.

Thus says the LORD of hosts: In those days ten men from the nations of every tongue shall take hold of the robe of a Jew, saying, 'Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.'"

The book of Zechariah's middle section ends with this picture. Foreigners grab the corner of a Jewish man's coat and beg to be taken along, and the reason they give is: we have heard that God is with you.

It happened. Salvation came to the world through the Jewish people, as Jesus told the Samaritan woman: salvation is from the Jews (John 4:22). Gentiles who were strangers to the covenants of promise have been brought near by the blood of Christ (Eph 2:12-13), and today most Christians on earth are among those who took hold of the robe.

And the reason still stands. What draws people is not our arguments or our buildings but the report that God is with us. That was the promise of 2:10 and 8:3, and it remains the church's only real attraction.

8.title: Old Men and Children in the Streets
8.overview:
God declares that he is jealous for Zion with great jealousy, has returned to Zion and will dwell in Jerusalem, which will be called the faithful city (vv. 1-3). Old men and old women will sit in its streets with staffs in hand, and the streets will be full of boys and girls playing (vv. 4-5). If that seems marvellous to the remnant, need it be marvellous to God? (v. 6). He will save his people from east and west and bring them to dwell in Jerusalem: they shall be his people and he their God, in faithfulness and righteousness (vv. 7-8).

Let the builders' hands be strong. Before, there was no wage for man or beast and no safety, and God set every man against his neighbour; but now there will be a sowing of peace, with vine, ground and heavens yielding again (vv. 9-12). As they were a byword of cursing, so God will save them and make them a blessing; fear not, let your hands be strong (v. 13). As he purposed disaster and did not relent, so he has purposed good (vv. 14-15). Therefore: speak the truth, render true judgments that make for peace, devise no evil in the heart, and love no false oath (vv. 16-17).

The fasts of the fourth, fifth, seventh and tenth months will become seasons of joy and cheerful feasts; therefore love truth and peace (vv. 18-19). Peoples from many cities will urge each other to go and seek the LORD, and many strong nations will come (vv. 20-22). In those days ten men from every tongue will take hold of the robe of a Jew and say, "Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you" (v. 23).
8.theology:
God is jealous for his people with a husband's protectiveness (v. 2).

God's measure of a restored society is the safety of the very old and the very young (vv. 4-5).

What seems impossible to God's people is not therefore impossible to God (v. 6; Luke 1:37).

The covenant promise stands: they shall be my people and I will be their God, and God keeps it in faithfulness and righteousness (v. 8; Jer 31:33; Rev 21:3).

The reliability God showed in his warnings is the measure of the reliability of his promises (vv. 14-15).

God's blessing calls for truthful speech, honest courts and hearts that scheme no evil (vv. 16-17).

God turns the anniversaries of his people's worst griefs into feasts (v. 19).

The nations come to God through the people God is with, fulfilled as Gentiles are brought near in Christ (vv. 20-23; John 4:22; Eph 2:12-13).
8.examples:
Old people with walking sticks sitting out in the street again.

Streets too safe to keep the children indoors.

A promise that looks impossible to everyone except God.

A sowing whose crop is peace.

A nation that was a byword for ruin turned into a blessing.

Four fast days turned into four festivals.

One neighbour saying to another: I myself am going.

Strangers holding the hem of a coat and asking to come along.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Oracle Against the Nations
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God's word moves down the map: Hadrach, Damascus, Hamath, then Tyre and Sidon, though they are very wise, whose heaped silver will not save her (vv. 1-4). The Philistine cities see and tremble (vv. 5-6), and then something unexpected: Philistia too shall be a remnant for our God, like a clan in Judah (v. 7). God will encamp at my house as a guard, for now I see with my own eyes (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: God judges the proud nations and then takes some of them into his own family, while guarding his people himself.

verseByVerse.quote: The oracle of the word of the LORD is against the land of Hadrach and Damascus is its resting place. For the LORD has an eye on mankind and on all the tribes of Israel, and on Hamath also, which borders on it, Tyre and Sidon, though they are very wise. Tyre has built herself a rampart and heaped up silver like dust, and fine gold like the mud of the streets. But behold, the Lord will strip her of her possessions and strike down her power on the sea, and she shall be devoured by fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The oracle of the word of the LORD is against the land of Hadrach and Damascus is its resting place. For the LORD has an eye on mankind and on all the tribes of Israel,

The last six chapters of Zechariah are different from the first eight: no dates, no visions, no named officials, just two long oracles (chapters 9-11 and 12-14) looking far into the future.

This one begins with a tour of the map, starting in the north with Hadrach and Damascus in Syria. And the reason given is that God's eye is on everyone (the ESV notes an alternative reading: "For the eye of mankind, especially of all the tribes of Israel, is toward the LORD").

and on Hamath also, which borders on it, Tyre and Sidon, though they are very wise.

Tyre has built herself a rampart and heaped up silver like dust, and fine gold like the mud of the streets.

But behold, the Lord will strip her of her possessions and strike down her power on the sea, and she shall be devoured by fire.

Tyre was the great trading port, famously clever and famously rich: silver like dust and gold like mud. Her island fortress had held out against siege after siege. And the verdict is four words long: she will be devoured by fire. Alexander the Great took the city in 332 BC by building a causeway out to the island.

Cleverness and money are real advantages, and they are no defence at all against God.

Notice that the oracle starts outside Israel and works inward. God's dealings with the nations are not a footnote to his dealings with his people; they are the same story.

verseByVerse.quote: Ashkelon shall see it, and be afraid; Gaza too, and shall writhe in anguish; Ekron also, because its hopes are confounded. The king shall perish from Gaza; Ashkelon shall be uninhabited; a mixed people shall dwell in Ashdod, and I will cut off the pride of Philistia. I will take away its blood from its mouth, and its abominations from between its teeth; it too shall be a remnant for our God; it shall be like a clan in Judah, and Ekron shall be like the Jebusites. Then I will encamp at my house as a guard, so that none shall march to and fro; no oppressor shall again march over them, for now I see with my own eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ashkelon shall see it, and be afraid; Gaza too, and shall writhe in anguish; Ekron also, because its hopes are confounded. The king shall perish from Gaza; Ashkelon shall be uninhabited;

a mixed people shall dwell in Ashdod, and I will cut off the pride of Philistia.

The Philistine cities watch Tyre fall and panic. (The ESV notes a mixed people may be "a foreign people".) Their pride is what God cuts off.

I will take away its blood from its mouth, and its abominations from between its teeth; it too shall be a remnant for our God; it shall be like a clan in Judah, and Ekron shall be like the Jebusites.

And now the surprise that changes the whole oracle. God takes the blood of pagan sacrifices out of Philistia's mouth, and then says: it too shall be a remnant for our God.

Philistia, the old enemy, becomes like a clan in Judah, an ordinary family among God's people. Ekron shall be like the Jebusites, the people of Jerusalem before David took it, who were absorbed into Israel.

This is the gospel in advance. God does not only defeat his enemies; he converts them and adopts them. Every Christian from a pagan background is an instance of it.

Then I will encamp at my house as a guard, so that none shall march to and fro; no oppressor shall again march over them, for now I see with my own eyes.

God pitches his tent around his house like a soldier on watch. The little temple they had just finished is guarded by God himself. Now I see with my own eyes: he has been watching all along.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–13 — Your King Comes, Humble on a Donkey
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion! Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey (v. 9). He will scrap the chariot and the war horse and speak peace to the nations, ruling from sea to sea (v. 10). Because of the blood of my covenant with you, I will set your prisoners free from the waterless pit (v. 11): prisoners of hope are promised double (vv. 12-13).
verseByVerse.theology: The king comes in humility, disarms his own people, rules the world and frees prisoners by the blood of his covenant.

verseByVerse.quote: Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion! Shout aloud, O daughter of Jerusalem! Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey. I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim and the war horse from Jerusalem; and the battle bow shall be cut off, and he shall speak peace to the nations; his rule shall be from sea to sea, and from the River to the ends of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion! Shout aloud, O daughter of Jerusalem! Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.

This is one of the great verses of the Old Testament, and Christians read it with the Gospels open.

Begin with the command: Rejoice greatly, Shout aloud. The reason for the joy is not a victory won or a harvest gathered, but a person arriving.

Behold, your king is coming to you. Not summoning them to him; coming to them. That is the direction of the whole Bible's story.

Then four things about him. He is righteous: everything he does is right. He is having salvation: he arrives carrying rescue, not demanding it. He is humble. And he is mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.

A conquering king rode a war horse; a donkey was the mount of a man coming in peace. So the king of the world arrives on a farm animal.

On the Sunday before he died, Jesus sent two disciples for a colt and rode it into Jerusalem while crowds spread their cloaks in the road. Matthew quotes this verse and says it happened to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet (Matt 21:5); John quotes it too (John 12:15). Five hundred years earlier, God had described the transport.

And the humility was not a costume. The king who rode in on a donkey was crucified on Friday. He is still the only king worth shouting for.

I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim and the war horse from Jerusalem; and the battle bow shall be cut off, and he shall speak peace to the nations; his rule shall be from sea to sea, and from the River to the ends of the earth.

Notice whose weapons are destroyed. Not the enemy's: the chariot from Ephraim and the war horse from Jerusalem. God's own people are disarmed, because their king does not need them and their security no longer depends on them.

What he does instead is speak peace to the nations. His weapon is his word, and the result is a rule that runs from sea to sea, and from the River (the ESV notes this means the Euphrates) to the ends of the earth.

That is happening now, wherever the gospel is preached and people submit gladly to Christ. It is not spread by force, and it never has been when it has been true to its king.

verseByVerse.quote: As for you also, because of the blood of my covenant with you, I will set your prisoners free from the waterless pit. Return to your stronghold, O prisoners of hope; today I declare that I will restore to you double. For I have bent Judah as my bow; I have made Ephraim its arrow. I will stir up your sons, O Zion, against your sons, O Greece, and wield you like a warrior's sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for you also, because of the blood of my covenant with you, I will set your prisoners free from the waterless pit.

A waterless pit was a dry cistern used as a dungeon; Joseph was thrown into one, and so was Jeremiah. It is a picture of hopeless captivity: deep, dry, and impossible to climb out of.

And the ground of the release is the striking phrase the blood of my covenant with you. At Sinai Moses had thrown blood on the people and said, Behold the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you (Exod 24:8).

On the night before he died, Jesus took a cup and said, this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins (Matt 26:28). That is how the prisoners get out of the pit. Not by climbing, but by blood.

Return to your stronghold, O prisoners of hope; today I declare that I will restore to you double.

Prisoners of hope is a wonderful phrase: people still in the pit, but with hope, because a promise has been made. That describes the Christian life exactly, lived between the promise and its completion.

And the promise is double, which is what Isaiah promised too: instead of your shame there shall be a double portion (Isa 61:7). God's restorations are not grudging repayments; they overflow.

For I have bent Judah as my bow; I have made Ephraim its arrow. I will stir up your sons, O Zion, against your sons, O Greece, and wield you like a warrior's sword.

God takes his people as his weapons: Judah the bow, Ephraim the arrow, Zion the sword in his hand. The mention of Greece is remarkable in the Persian period, when Greece was not yet the world power it became.

Under the new covenant the church's weapons are not swords, and our warfare is not against flesh and blood. But the picture holds: God does his work in the world through his people, and he is the one wielding them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–17 — The LORD Will Save Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD will appear over them and march out in the storm (v. 14). He will protect his people until they are filled like a festival bowl (v. 15). On that day the LORD their God will save them, as the flock of his people; for like the jewels of a crown they shall shine on his land (v. 16). For how great is his goodness, and how great his beauty! (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: God fights for his people and then wears them like jewels in a crown.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD will appear over them, and his arrow will go forth like lightning; the Lord GOD will sound the trumpet and will march forth in the whirlwinds of the south. The LORD of hosts will protect them, and they shall devour, and tread down the sling stones, and they shall drink and roar as if drunk with wine, and be full like a bowl, drenched like the corners of the altar. On that day the LORD their God will save them, as the flock of his people; for like the jewels of a crown they shall shine on his land. For how great is his goodness, and how great his beauty! Grain shall make the young men flourish, and new wine the young women.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the LORD will appear over them, and his arrow will go forth like lightning; the Lord GOD will sound the trumpet and will march forth in the whirlwinds of the south.

The scene becomes a storm. God appears over them, his arrow flashes like lightning, he blows the trumpet himself and marches out in the desert whirlwinds. This is the God who came down at Sinai, fighting for a small people.

The LORD of hosts will protect them, and they shall devour, and tread down the sling stones, and they shall drink and roar as if drunk with wine, and be full like a bowl, drenched like the corners of the altar.

The imagery is rough and jubilant: victory so complete that the enemy's sling stones are trodden underfoot, and the victors are as noisy as men at a feast, full like a bowl used to catch sacrificial blood at the altar.

On that day the LORD their God will save them, as the flock of his people; for like the jewels of a crown they shall shine on his land.

And then the tone changes completely, and this is the loveliest verse of the chapter. The people God has just wielded as weapons are now the flock of his people, saved by their shepherd, and like the jewels of a crown they shall shine on his land.

Think about that. God wears his people as a king wears his crown jewels. The same community that had been squabbling about fast days and struggling with a half-built temple is God's public treasure. Malachi will say something similar: they will be his treasured possession.

For how great is his goodness, and how great his beauty! Grain shall make the young men flourish, and new wine the young women.

The chapter ends in worship: how great is his goodness, and how great his beauty! After all the storm and war, the prophet's final reaction is to admire God.

And the last picture is young people flourishing on good food and new wine: a society with a future, which is exactly what a struggling remnant needed to be promised.

9.title: Behold, Your King Is Coming
9.overview:
The oracle moves against Hadrach, Damascus and Hamath, and against Tyre and Sidon, wise and rich, whose heaped silver and gold will not prevent her being stripped and burned (vv. 1-4). Ashkelon, Gaza and Ekron see it and are afraid; Philistia's pride is cut off, and yet Philistia too will become a remnant for God, like a clan in Judah (vv. 5-7). God will encamp at his house as a guard, so that no oppressor marches over them again (v. 8).

Zion is told to rejoice greatly: her king is coming, righteous and having salvation, humble and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey (v. 9). He will cut off chariot, war horse and battle bow, speak peace to the nations, and rule from sea to sea (v. 10). Because of the blood of God's covenant, prisoners will be freed from the waterless pit, and prisoners of hope are promised double (vv. 11-12). God will bend Judah as his bow, make Ephraim its arrow and wield Zion like a sword against Greece (v. 13).

The LORD will appear over them, his arrow like lightning, marching in the whirlwinds of the south; he will protect them until they are full like a bowl (vv. 14-15). On that day he will save them as the flock of his people, and like the jewels of a crown they will shine on his land. How great is his goodness and his beauty, with grain for the young men and new wine for the young women (vv. 16-17).
9.theology:
Wealth and cleverness are no defence against God (vv. 2-4).

God not only defeats his enemies but converts and adopts them into his people (v. 7).

God himself stands guard over his house and his people (v. 8).

The promised king comes to his people, righteous, bringing salvation, and humble — fulfilled when Jesus rode into Jerusalem (v. 9; Matt 21:5; John 12:15).

The king disarms his own people and rules the world by speaking peace (v. 10).

Prisoners are set free by the blood of God's covenant, which Christ named at the last supper (v. 11; Exod 24:8; Matt 26:28).

Believers live as prisoners of hope between the promise and its completion, and God's restoration is double (v. 12; Isa 61:7).

God saves his people as a flock and displays them as the jewels of his crown (v. 16).
9.examples:
An island fortress with silver heaped like dust, burned to the ground.

Old enemies absorbed into God's family like an ordinary clan.

God pitching his tent around a modest temple as a guard.

A world king arriving on a borrowed farm animal.

God's own chariots and war horses scrapped as unnecessary.

A dry cistern with no way out, and a door opened by blood.

Prisoners who still have hope because a promise has been made.

God wearing his people like the jewels of a crown.

The pride of Assyria shall be laid low, and the scepter of Egypt shall depart.<sup>12</sup>I will make them strong in the LORD, and they shall walk in his name," declares the LORD.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ask rain from the LORD in the season of the spring rain (v. 1), because household gods and diviners give empty consolation, and so the people wander like sheep; they are afflicted for lack of a shepherd (v. 2). God's anger is hot against the shepherds, for the LORD of hosts cares for his flock (v. 3). From Judah will come the cornerstone, the tent peg, the battle bow and every ruler (v. 4), and the flock will fight like mighty men because the LORD is with them (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: People who will not ask God for rain end up consulting anything, and God holds their leaders responsible.

verseByVerse.quote: Ask rain from the LORD in the season of the spring rain, from the LORD who makes the storm clouds, and he will give them showers of rain, to everyone the vegetation in the field. For the household gods utter nonsense, and the diviners see lies; they tell false dreams and give empty consolation. Therefore the people wander like sheep; they are afflicted for lack of a shepherd. "My anger is hot against the shepherds, and I will punish the leaders; for the LORD of hosts cares for his flock, the house of Judah, and will make them like his majestic steed in battle. From him shall come the cornerstone, from him the tent peg, from him the battle bow, from him every ruler— all of them together. They shall be like mighty men in battle, trampling the foe in the mud of the streets; they shall fight because the LORD is with them, and they shall put to shame the riders on horses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ask rain from the LORD in the season of the spring rain, from the LORD who makes the storm clouds, and he will give them showers of rain, to everyone the vegetation in the field.

A farming community lived or died by the spring rain that filled out the grain before harvest. The temptation was to secure it by the methods the neighbouring nations used: charms, household gods, fertility rites.

God's instruction is startlingly simple: Ask. Ask him, because he is the LORD who makes the storm clouds. The alternative to superstition is not self-reliance; it is prayer.

For the household gods utter nonsense, and the diviners see lies; they tell false dreams and give empty consolation. Therefore the people wander like sheep; they are afflicted for lack of a shepherd.

Here is the verdict on every substitute for God: nonsense, lies, false dreams, empty consolation. That last phrase is the saddest. The horoscope, the charm, the confident guru: they do console, briefly, and the comfort is empty.

And the consequence is a community of sheep with no shepherd, wandering and afflicted. When Jesus looked at the crowds he saw exactly this: they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd (Matt 9:36). And he did something about it.

"My anger is hot against the shepherds, and I will punish the leaders; for the LORD of hosts cares for his flock, the house of Judah, and will make them like his majestic steed in battle.

God's anger burns against the shepherds, the leaders who should have fed the flock (the ESV notes the Hebrew calls them "the male goats", the ones who push to the front). And the reason is stated: the LORD of hosts cares for his flock. God's anger at bad shepherds is a function of his love for the sheep.

Then a transformation: the frightened flock becomes his majestic steed in battle, God's own warhorse. He does not merely pity the weak; he makes them formidable.

From him shall come the cornerstone, from him the tent peg, from him the battle bow, from him every ruler— all of them together.

Four images of leadership, and all four come from him, that is, from Judah's own people rather than from foreign patrons. The cornerstone holds a building square; the tent peg is what everything hangs on; the battle bow defends; the ruler governs.

Christians recognise all four in one person. Christ is the cornerstone on whom the whole building is joined together (Eph 2:20), the peg on whom everything hangs, the defender and the ruler. And he came from Judah.

They shall be like mighty men in battle, trampling the foe in the mud of the streets; they shall fight because the LORD is with them, and they shall put to shame the riders on horses.

The secret of their strength is in the middle of the verse: because the LORD is with them. Not better equipment; better company.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–12 — I Will Whistle for Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I will strengthen the house of Judah, and I will save the house of Joseph, restoring them as though I had not rejected them (vv. 6-7). I will whistle for them and gather them in, for I have redeemed them (v. 8); scattered among the nations, in far countries they shall remember me (v. 9). God will bring them home past every obstacle, laying low the pride of Assyria and Egypt (vv. 10-11), and I will make them strong in the LORD, and they shall walk in his name (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: God whistles for his scattered people like a shepherd calling a flock, and they come.

verseByVerse.quote: "I will strengthen the house of Judah, and I will save the house of Joseph. I will bring them back because I have compassion on them, and they shall be as though I had not rejected them, for I am the LORD their God and I will answer them. Then Ephraim shall become like a mighty warrior, and their hearts shall be glad as with wine. Their children shall see it and be glad; their hearts shall rejoice in the LORD. "I will whistle for them and gather them in, for I have redeemed them, and they shall be as many as they were before. Though I scattered them among the nations, yet in far countries they shall remember me, and with their children they shall live and return.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"I will strengthen the house of Judah, and I will save the house of Joseph. I will bring them back because I have compassion on them, and they shall be as though I had not rejected them, for I am the LORD their God and I will answer them.

Both halves of the divided nation are named: Judah in the south and Joseph in the north, whose people had been scattered by Assyria long before. God intends to have them all.

And then a phrase that is worth a long pause: they shall be as though I had not rejected them. Not "they will be tolerated", not "they will live with the consequences", but restored so completely that the rejection might never have happened.

That is what forgiveness in Christ does. The prodigal comes home and is given the robe and the ring, not a place among the hired servants.

Then Ephraim shall become like a mighty warrior, and their hearts shall be glad as with wine. Their children shall see it and be glad; their hearts shall rejoice in the LORD.

Notice the generations: Their children shall see it and be glad. What God does for one generation is meant to be watched by the next. Children who see their parents genuinely glad in God are being given something no lesson can supply.

"I will whistle for them and gather them in, for I have redeemed them, and they shall be as many as they were before.

A shepherd's whistle: a sound the flock knows, cutting across distance, and they come. It is a homely picture of what God does to gather his people out of the world, and it works because I have redeemed them. They are his already; the whistle is the call of an owner.

Jesus said, My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me (John 10:27). Every conversion is someone hearing the whistle.

Though I scattered them among the nations, yet in far countries they shall remember me, and with their children they shall live and return.

God takes responsibility for the scattering, and then promises that the scattering will not be the end: in far countries they shall remember me. Distance from home does not put anyone out of God's reach, and exile has often been the very place where people start remembering God.

verseByVerse.quote: I will bring them home from the land of Egypt, and gather them from Assyria, and I will bring them to the land of Gilead and to Lebanon, till there is no room for them. He shall pass through the sea of troubles and strike down the waves of the sea, and all the depths of the Nile shall be dried up. The pride of Assyria shall be laid low, and the scepter of Egypt shall depart. I will make them strong in the LORD, and they shall walk in his name," declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will bring them home from the land of Egypt, and gather them from Assyria, and I will bring them to the land of Gilead and to Lebanon, till there is no room for them.

Egypt and Assyria stand for the two great powers that had swallowed God's people. God will empty them both. And the return is so large that there will be no room for them, which is the happiest sort of problem.

He shall pass through the sea of troubles and strike down the waves of the sea, and all the depths of the Nile shall be dried up. The pride of Assyria shall be laid low, and the scepter of Egypt shall depart.

The language is deliberately the language of the exodus: a sea divided, the Nile dried up, Egypt humbled. God's past rescues are the pattern of his future ones, and he is not short of new exoduses.

I will make them strong in the LORD, and they shall walk in his name," declares the LORD.

The chapter ends with two phrases that sum up the Christian life. Strong in the LORD: the strength is real, and it is not our own; Paul tells the Ephesians to be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might. And they shall walk in his name: ordinary daily living, done as people who belong to him and bear his name.

A flock with no shepherd at the start of the chapter; a people walking in God's name at the end. That is the difference a shepherd makes.

10.title: Ask Rain from the LORD
10.overview:
Ask rain from the LORD in the season of the spring rain, for he makes the storm clouds and gives showers (v. 1). Household gods utter nonsense, diviners see lies and give empty consolation, so the people wander like sheep, afflicted for lack of a shepherd (v. 2). God's anger is hot against the shepherds and he will punish the leaders, for he cares for his flock and will make them like his majestic steed in battle (v. 3). From Judah will come the cornerstone, the tent peg, the battle bow and every ruler, and they will fight as mighty men because the LORD is with them (vv. 4-5).

God will strengthen Judah and save Joseph, bringing them back in compassion so that they are as though he had not rejected them; Ephraim will be glad, and their children will see it and rejoice (vv. 6-7). He will whistle for them and gather them in, for he has redeemed them; scattered among the nations, they will remember him in far countries and return with their children (vv. 8-9). He will bring them from Egypt and Assyria to Gilead and Lebanon until there is no room, passing through the sea of troubles, drying the Nile and laying low the pride of Assyria (vv. 10-11). He will make them strong in the LORD, and they shall walk in his name (v. 12).
10.theology:
The alternative to superstition is not self-reliance but asking God (v. 1).

Every substitute for God offers empty consolation and leaves people shepherdless (v. 2; Matt 9:36).

God's anger against bad shepherds flows from his care for the flock (v. 3).

God's leadership for his people comes from among them, and is fulfilled in Christ the cornerstone (v. 4; Eph 2:20).

The strength of God's people is his presence, not their equipment (v. 5).

God restores so completely that it is as though he had never rejected them (v. 6).

God calls his own like a shepherd whistling for his flock, because he has already redeemed them (v. 8; John 10:27).

Exile does not put anyone beyond God's reach; far countries are where people often start remembering him (v. 9).
10.examples:
Farmers tempted to buy rain from a charm instead of asking God.

Consolation that works for an evening and is empty by morning.

Leaders called the male goats that push to the front.

A frightened flock turned into God's own warhorse.

A people restored as though the rejection had never happened.

A shepherd's whistle carrying across a long distance.

So many coming home that there is no room for them.

11.text: <sup>1</sup>Open your doors, O Lebanon, that the fire may devour your cedars!<sup>2</sup>Wail, O cypress, for the cedar has fallen, for the glorious trees are ruined! Wail, oaks of Bashan, for the thick forest has been felled!<sup>3</sup>The sound of the wail of the shepherds, for their glory is ruined! The sound of the roar of the lions, for the thicket of the Jordan is ruined!<sup>4</sup>Thus said the LORD my God: "Become shepherd of the flock doomed to slaughter.<sup>5</sup>Those who buy them slaughter them and go unpunished, and those who sell them say, 'Blessed be the LORD, I have become rich,' and their own shepherds have no pity on them.<sup>6</sup>For I will no longer have pity on the inhabitants of this land, declares the LORD. Behold, I will cause each of them to fall into the hand of his neighbor, and each into the hand of his king, and they shall crush the land, and I will deliver none from their hand."<sup>7</sup>So I became the shepherd of the flock doomed to be slaughtered by the sheep traders. And I took two staffs, one I named Favor, the other I named Union. And I tended the sheep.<sup>8</sup>In one month I destroyed the three shepherds. But I became impatient with them, and they also detested me.<sup>9</sup>So I said, "I will not be your shepherd. What is to die, let it die. What is to be destroyed, let it be destroyed. And let those who are left devour the flesh of one another."<sup>10</sup>And I took my staff Favor, and I broke it, annulling the covenant that I had made with all the peoples.<sup>11</sup>So it was annulled on that day, and the sheep traders, who were watching me, knew that it was the word of the LORD.<sup>12</sup>Then I said to them, "If it seems good to you, give me my wages; but if not, keep them." And they weighed out as my wages thirty pieces of silver.<sup>13</sup>Then the LORD said to me, "Throw it to the potter"— the lordly price at which I was priced by them.
