verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Open your doors, O Lebanon, that the fire may devour your cedars! (v. 1). Cypress, oak and thicket are ruined, and the shepherds and the lions wail over their lost glory (vv. 2-3). God tells the prophet, Become shepherd of the flock doomed to slaughter, whose buyers kill them and whose sellers bless God for their profits (vv. 4-5). God will no longer pity the land (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: When leaders treat people as merchandise, God hands the people over to what they have chosen.

verseByVerse.quote: Open your doors, O Lebanon, that the fire may devour your cedars! Wail, O cypress, for the cedar has fallen, for the glorious trees are ruined! Wail, oaks of Bashan, for the thick forest has been felled! The sound of the wail of the shepherds, for their glory is ruined! The sound of the roar of the lions, for the thicket of the Jordan is ruined! Thus said the LORD my God: "Become shepherd of the flock doomed to slaughter. Those who buy them slaughter them and go unpunished, and those who sell them say, 'Blessed be the LORD, I have become rich,' and their own shepherds have no pity on them. For I will no longer have pity on the inhabitants of this land, declares the LORD. Behold, I will cause each of them to fall into the hand of his neighbor, and each into the hand of his king, and they shall crush the land, and I will deliver none from their hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Open your doors, O Lebanon, that the fire may devour your cedars!

Wail, O cypress, for the cedar has fallen, for the glorious trees are ruined! Wail, oaks of Bashan, for the thick forest has been felled!

The sound of the wail of the shepherds, for their glory is ruined! The sound of the roar of the lions, for the thicket of the Jordan is ruined!

The chapter opens with a forest fire running from the cedars of Lebanon in the north to the thicket of the Jordan. Great trees are the Bible's regular picture for great men, and here they come down.

Then the sound: first the wail of the shepherds, the leaders who have lost their pastures, and then the roar of the lions, the predators who have lost their cover. When judgment comes, both the careless leaders and the ones who preyed on the flock are left with nothing.

Thus said the LORD my God: "Become shepherd of the flock doomed to slaughter.

Now Zechariah is given a part to play, and it is a terrible one: Become shepherd of the flock doomed to slaughter. Prophets often acted out their messages, and this is one of the darkest.

Those who buy them slaughter them and go unpunished, and those who sell them say, 'Blessed be the LORD, I have become rich,' and their own shepherds have no pity on them.

Three groups are named, and all three are guilty. The buyers slaughter them and go unpunished. The sellers thank God for their profits: Blessed be the LORD, I have become rich — religious language over a trade in human beings. And their own shepherds have no pity.

The combination of piety and exploitation is one of the ugliest things in the Bible, and it is common enough to need naming. People still bless God for gains made at others' cost.

For I will no longer have pity on the inhabitants of this land, declares the LORD. Behold, I will cause each of them to fall into the hand of his neighbor, and each into the hand of his king, and they shall crush the land, and I will deliver none from their hand."

The judgment is to be handed over to what they have chosen: neighbours and kings who will crush the land. Sometimes God's severest act is to stop protecting people from the consequences of their own preferences.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prophet shepherds the doomed flock with two staffs, Favor and Union (v. 7). He removes three shepherds, and shepherd and flock come to detest each other (vv. 8-9). He breaks Favor, annulling the covenant (vv. 10-11), asks for his wages and is weighed out thirty pieces of silver, which God tells him to Throw ... to the potter (vv. 12-13). Then he breaks Union (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: The good shepherd is valued at the price of a slave, and the rejection of him breaks both grace and unity.

verseByVerse.quote: So I became the shepherd of the flock doomed to be slaughtered by the sheep traders. And I took two staffs, one I named Favor, the other I named Union. And I tended the sheep. In one month I destroyed the three shepherds. But I became impatient with them, and they also detested me. So I said, "I will not be your shepherd. What is to die, let it die. What is to be destroyed, let it be destroyed. And let those who are left devour the flesh of one another." And I took my staff Favor, and I broke it, annulling the covenant that I had made with all the peoples. So it was annulled on that day, and the sheep traders, who were watching me, knew that it was the word of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I became the shepherd of the flock doomed to be slaughtered by the sheep traders. And I took two staffs, one I named Favor, the other I named Union. And I tended the sheep.

The prophet takes up the job with two shepherd's staffs, and their names tell us what God had been giving his people. Favor is his grace, the covenant kindness that kept them. Union is the bond that held Judah and Israel together as one people.

And notice the quiet line: And I tended the sheep. He did the work properly.

In one month I destroyed the three shepherds. But I became impatient with them, and they also detested me.

Three bad shepherds are removed quickly. Commentators have guessed at their identity for centuries, and the text does not say; it is wiser to leave it.

What matters is the relationship: they also detested me. The flock hated the shepherd who was actually caring for them. That is a sentence with a long shadow, and it falls across the Gospels.

So I said, "I will not be your shepherd. What is to die, let it die. What is to be destroyed, let it be destroyed. And let those who are left devour the flesh of one another."

The shepherd resigns, and the result is a flock that turns on itself. A community that rejects God's care does not become free; it becomes self-consuming.

And I took my staff Favor, and I broke it, annulling the covenant that I had made with all the peoples.

So it was annulled on that day, and the sheep traders, who were watching me, knew that it was the word of the LORD.

The staff called Favor is snapped across the knee. God's restraining protection over the nations, which had kept his people from being destroyed, is withdrawn.

Only the sheep traders understand what they are seeing. The people at the bottom of the trade usually see the spiritual reality more clearly than the men at the top.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I said to them, "If it seems good to you, give me my wages; but if not, keep them." And they weighed out as my wages thirty pieces of silver. Then the LORD said to me, "Throw it to the potter"— the lordly price at which I was priced by them. So I took the thirty pieces of silver and threw them into the house of the LORD, to the potter. Then I broke my second staff Union, annulling the brotherhood between Judah and Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I said to them, "If it seems good to you, give me my wages; but if not, keep them." And they weighed out as my wages thirty pieces of silver.

The shepherd asks to be paid, and leaves the amount to them. What he receives is a calculated insult: thirty pieces of silver. The law of Moses set thirty shekels as the compensation for a slave gored by someone's ox (Exod 21:32). That is what they thought his care was worth: the price of a dead slave.

Then the LORD said to me, "Throw it to the potter"— the lordly price at which I was priced by them. So I took the thirty pieces of silver and threw them into the house of the LORD, to the potter.

The phrase the lordly price is heavy with sarcasm. And the money is thrown away, into the temple, to the potter.

Every Christian reader knows where this reappears. Judas agreed to betray Jesus for thirty pieces of silver (Matt 26:15), then threw the coins into the temple, and the priests used them to buy a potter's field. Matthew records it as the fulfilment of prophecy (Matt 27:9-10).

Matthew attributes the quotation to Jeremiah the prophet, though the words are found here in Zechariah. Christians have explained this in various ways: that Matthew is blending Zechariah's words with Jeremiah's potter and field passages, that he names the scroll in which Jeremiah stood first among the prophets, or that a copying error entered early. Nobody can be certain, and honesty is better than pretending. What is certain is that the details of the betrayal of Jesus were written down five centuries before, down to the amount and what became of the coins.

Let the weight of it land. The Good Shepherd was priced at the going rate for a slave, by the people he came to save.

Then I broke my second staff Union, annulling the brotherhood between Judah and Israel.

The second staff goes too. Having rejected the shepherd, the flock loses its unity. That is the order: reject Christ, and the bonds between people begin to fail as well.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God tells the prophet to take the equipment of a foolish shepherd (v. 15), because he is raising up one who will not seek the young or heal the maimed or nourish the healthy, but devours the flock (v. 16). Woe to my worthless shepherd, who deserts the flock! (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: A people who reject the shepherd God sends will get the shepherd they deserve.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to me, "Take once more the equipment of a foolish shepherd. For behold, I am raising up in the land a shepherd who does not care for those being destroyed, or seek the young or heal the maimed or nourish the healthy, but devours the flesh of the fat ones, tearing off even their hoofs. "Woe to my worthless shepherd, who deserts the flock! May the sword strike his arm and his right eye! Let his arm be wholly withered, his right eye utterly blinded!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the LORD said to me, "Take once more the equipment of a foolish shepherd.

A second piece of acting, and worse than the first. The prophet must now play a bad shepherd.

For behold, I am raising up in the land a shepherd who does not care for those being destroyed, or seek the young or heal the maimed or nourish the healthy, but devours the flesh of the fat ones, tearing off even their hoofs.

Read the list of what this shepherd does not do: he does not care for those being destroyed, does not seek the young, does not heal the maimed, does not nourish the healthy. Ezekiel had made the same charge against Israel's leaders (Ezek 34:4). What he does do is eat the best of the flock.

This is God's judgment on a people who rejected the shepherd he sent: they get the shepherd they preferred. It is a frightening principle. Leaders are often what a community has asked for.

"Woe to my worthless shepherd, who deserts the flock! May the sword strike his arm and his right eye! Let his arm be wholly withered, his right eye utterly blinded!"

The chapter ends with a curse on the false shepherd: the arm that should have defended the sheep withered, the eye that should have watched them blinded. God does not treat the abuse of the vulnerable lightly.

And the whole dark chapter leaves us needing a shepherd who is the opposite of this one. Jesus said, I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). Here the shepherd deserts the flock and is struck; there the Shepherd is struck and does not desert. That contrast is the mercy this chapter drives us toward.

11.title: Thirty Pieces of Silver
11.overview:
Fire is called to devour the cedars of Lebanon; cypress and oaks wail as the forest falls, and the shepherds and lions wail over their ruined glory (vv. 1-3). God tells the prophet to become shepherd of the flock doomed to slaughter, whose buyers kill them unpunished and whose sellers bless the LORD for their riches, while their own shepherds have no pity; God will no longer pity the land but hand them to neighbours and kings (vv. 4-6).

The prophet shepherds the flock with two staffs named Favor and Union. He destroys three shepherds in one month, becomes impatient with the flock, and they detest him; so he resigns them to their fate (vv. 7-9). He breaks Favor, annulling the covenant, and the sheep traders recognise the word of the LORD (vv. 10-11). He asks for his wages and is weighed out thirty pieces of silver, which God tells him to throw to the potter, and he throws them into the house of the LORD (vv. 12-13). Then he breaks Union, annulling the brotherhood between Judah and Israel (v. 14).

God tells him to take the equipment of a foolish shepherd, for he is raising up a shepherd who will not care for the perishing, seek the young, heal the maimed or feed the healthy, but will devour the flock (vv. 15-16). Woe to that worthless shepherd who deserts the flock: may his arm wither and his right eye be blinded (v. 17).
11.theology:
When leaders treat people as merchandise, and bless God for the profits, God sees both the trade and the piety (v. 5).

God's severest judgment can be to stop protecting people from what they have chosen (v. 6).

A flock that rejects its shepherd does not become free but self-consuming (v. 9).

God's favour and the unity of his people are gifts that can be withdrawn (vv. 10, 14).

The shepherd God sends is valued at the price of a dead slave, fulfilled in the betrayal of Jesus for thirty pieces of silver (vv. 12-13; Exod 21:32; Matt 26:15; 27:9-10).

Those who reject the true shepherd receive the shepherd they preferred (vv. 15-16; Ezek 34:4).

God curses shepherds who desert and devour the flock, and sends the Good Shepherd who lays down his life for it (v. 17; John 10:11).
11.examples:
A forest fire running the length of a country, and the lions losing their cover.

Sellers thanking God for the profits of a trade in lives.

Two shepherd's staffs, named Favor and Union.

A flock that comes to detest the shepherd who feeds it.

Wages weighed out at the compensation rate for a dead slave.

Coins thrown into the temple and used to buy a field.

A shepherd's arm withered and his watching eye blinded.
